title: Runoff, Return Solution & Root-Zone EC Interpretation

content.overview: Runoff or return solution provides useful information but is not a complete picture of root-zone conditions. Volume, timing, sampling method, preferential flow and spatial concentration can all change what a runoff or return sample represents.

vocabulary.definition: The portion of applied irrigation volume collected as drainage under the defined measurement method.
Solution leaving or returning from the root-zone system after interacting with the crop and media.
Water movement through limited pathways that can bypass parts of the root zone.

sections.title: Runoff does not prove uniform wetting
sections.body: Drainage can begin while portions of the root zone remain relatively dry, especially where channels or uneven distribution exist.

sections.title: Return EC reflects multiple processes
sections.body: Rising return/root-zone EC can reflect concentration from water loss, selective uptake, uneven delivery or accumulation. Stable input EC does not guarantee stable root-zone chemistry.

sections.title: Sampling method must stay consistent
sections.body: First-drain, composite and late-drain samples can differ. Record timing, location and collection method so trends remain interpretable.

workedExamples: A high return EC from a dry corner of one slab should not automatically be generalized to the whole room without representative comparison.
commonMistakes: Treating return EC as a direct nutrient formulation test.
content.practicalApplication: Compare input, root-zone and runoff/return data from three zones and identify whether the strongest concern is concentration, poor distribution, sampling bias or unresolved.
content.summary: Runoff and return data are evidence streams that need volume, timing and spatial context.
